The ownership direction is coherent, but durable task recovery introduces application state that needs an explicit owner before selecting a sandbox mechanism. The existing boundaries are useful: fleet admission remains with the daemon, tools execute behind the engine boundary, and conversation compaction remains independent of the guest (`concepts_brief.md:32–54`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:46–72`). No Blocker is established at brainstorm depth.

References below are rooted at `/Users/kishore/Projects/agentsfleet-approved-fleet-chat`; `SPACE/` means `/Users/kishore/Projects/oss/rs/SPACE`.

**Major — Long-Term Tech Debt & Maintainability: task recovery needs one application owner across several differently scoped stores.**

The concept introduces a coding session spanning leases, then associates conversation progress and command outcomes with a saved workspace generation (`concepts_brief.md:119–135`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:124–156`). The storage owner remains explicitly unselected (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:412`).

Existing identities differ deliberately. Runtime compaction uses fleet, lease and branch identity (`rustd/crates/afr_agent/src/loop/context/mod.rs:92–130`); storage uniquely keys runtime notes by lease and branch (`schema/2160_memory_context_checkpoints.sql:13–30`). Semantic memory instead hydrates by fleet (`rustd/crates/afd_fleet/src/lease/memory.rs:57–72`). Held checkout identity also names the fleet without a task or incident (`rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/holds/mod.rs:36–49`).

The maintenance risk is implementing session recovery separately in each adapter. That creates several competing answers to which conversation, files and outcomes may resume after a crash. A newer conversation can describe files absent from the last completed save. Fleet memory can intentionally contain lessons from earlier incidents; it must not become the record that selects another incident’s workspace or approval.

Counterargument: the evaluation already distinguishes recovery units and demands generation linkage (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:93–120`, `154–168`). That is the right requirement; a finished schema is unnecessary for this review.

Concept requirement: name the application owner of task identity, authoritative recovery selection and the mapping between saved workspace generation, source history and confirmed outcomes. Explicitly distinguish that state from advisory fleet memory. Preserve fleet learning without treating it as incident authority. Keep existing compaction identity checks intact until an authorized handoff supplies the new scope.

Later proof: recover A after B and worker replacement, including newer conversation history with an older file checkpoint, missing command results and fleet memory mentioning both incidents.

**Major — Long-Term Tech Debt & Maintainability: a continuing repair session does not yet have continuing publication identity.**

The proposed repair journey preserves local work across leases and reconciles existing remote drafts, while duplicate chat and Slack approvals must resolve to one repair admission (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:124–160`, `249–255`, `275–297`).

Current publication identity is derived from the admitted event: delivery passes that event to `repair_branch` (`rustd/crates/afd_fleet/src/lease/deliver/mod.rs:52`, `228–238`), and `branch_for` encodes it directly (`rustd/crates/afd_gate/src/policy/repair.rs:65–66`). The write rules admit creation of that exact ref and a draft using that head; they do not provide an update path for an existing ref (`rustd/crates/afd_gate/src/policy/egress/write.rs:83–109`).

A repair session can therefore retain the same files while a subsequent admission receives another publication identity. Conversely, resuming the original identity after its draft exists cannot silently imply permission to update that branch. These are different product outcomes, not interchangeable retry techniques.

Counterargument: reclaiming the same unfinished admission can retain its identity. The uncertainty concerns ordinary follow-ups, refreshed proposals and later approved attempts, rather than every worker replacement.

Concept requirement: define how a repair attempt relates to its proposal, admissions and daemon-issued publication identity. State whether a published draft ends that attempt, and what a subsequently approved change means under the existing publication limits. Keep distinct incidents separate. The owner must choose these outcomes; durable files alone cannot settle them.

Later proof: lose the acknowledgement after draft creation, replace the worker, approve through both channels, then send a later follow-up. Verify that each outcome follows the chosen repair-attempt rules without widening publication rights.

**Major — Long-Term Tech Debt & Maintainability: approval-led repair needs an explicit entry rule alongside existing direct requests.**

The proposal requires a diagnosis-linked approval before patch work and changes a failed workflow into diagnosis evidence rather than patch approval (`concepts_brief.md:88–100`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:236–239`, `261–297`).

Existing journeys authorize repair differently. The production scenario permits a failed workflow or human steer under the installed grant (`docs/architecture/scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md:36–44`). The Slack scenario expressly permits an addressed repair request without another approval (`docs/architecture/scenarios/slack-incident-responder.md:115–124`). Current lease delivery assembles write policy from fleet configuration, event identity and approved integration grants (`rustd/crates/afd_fleet/src/lease/deliver/mod.rs:44–66`).

Without an explicit selection rule, maintainers could put proposal checks into Slack routing while chat or workflow admission follows another path. Alternatively, a universal new check could accidentally remove the existing direct-request journey.

Counterargument: the evaluation clearly calls this a proposed incident flow and preserves repository grants as the access ceiling (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:239`, `283–297`). The unresolved point is which saved setup or work request selects that flow.

Concept requirement: record the entry rule for approval-led repair and its relationship to existing direct addressed requests and workflow triggers. Keep proposal resolution application-owned and shared across channels; provider adapters should deliver verified intent to that owner. Do not reuse a parked responder admission as the waiting proposal: that can block later work (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:329–331`).

Later proof: exercise each supported entry route, absent and ambiguous proposals, expired approval, and simultaneous answers. Preserve diagnosis-only outcomes, draft-only publication, human merge and the existing deployment pipeline.

**Major — Long-Term Tech Debt & Maintainability: durable sessions need storage and waiting-time budgets independent of compute holds.**

The concept allows several incidents and saved sessions under persistent fleets, with compute released while work waits for approval (`concepts_brief.md:102–135`). Retention, checkpoint frequency, evidence limits, queue capacity and diagnosis delay remain open (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:170–172`, `349–351`).

The existing documented workspace target retains three snapshots per fleet, while held compute expires after ten minutes and may be destroyed earlier (`docs/architecture/runner_execution.md:344–355`). Those fleet-level limits cannot directly represent several unfinished incident sessions. The current queue documentation also provides no global waiting-time guarantee and describes a per-fleet ceiling of 10,000 unsettled admissions (`docs/architecture/datastore_scaling.md:213–225`). A bounded queue count does not establish an acceptable critical-alert delay.

The maintenance risk is moving formerly temporary resources into durable storage without identifying who refuses, expires or deletes them. A busy fleet can accumulate approved repairs, waiting proposals, saved generations and incomplete uploads even when it runs only one lease.

Concept requirement: retain explicit owner decisions for maximum diagnosis start delay; queued repair capacity; active saved sessions; bytes and generations retained per session and tenant; checkpoint frequency and acceptable loss; retention duration; and cleanup reserve. Identify which owner applies each limit and what users see when it is reached. The benchmark concurrency values of 1, 10 and 100 are workloads, not operational limits (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:454–458`).

Later proof: reach the selected limits with several unfinished incidents, fail a save, expire compute and attempt stale deletion. Confirm that cleanup preserves each session’s last retained recoverable generation. No numerical budget or measured capacity is established by this review.

**Major — Long-Term Tech Debt & Maintainability: source maintenance and saved-state maintenance are separate obligations.**

The brief correctly requires provenance, dependency review and upstream fixes (`concepts_brief.md:24–30`, `162–164`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:416–444`). It does not yet state the compatibility lifetime of retained task state.

SPACE’s supervisor manifest imports shared service and runtime crates, enabling both host runtime and artifact storage (`SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/supervisor/Cargo.toml:32–35`). The runtime manifest adds further shared components and generated protocol support (`SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/core/Cargo.toml:13–18`, `43–53`). Its documentation explicitly excludes Rust crate interfaces from the service compatibility guarantee (`SPACE/docs/versioning.md:25–36`). A copied mechanism therefore has an independently maintained integration surface.

Saved state adds another burden. SPACE documents retaining compatible runtime and kernel artifacts for old snapshots and validating upgrade and rollback combinations (`SPACE/docs/versioning.md:89–115`). That is useful evidence of the ownership cost, not proof that `agentsfleet` needs the same policy. File checkpoints and complete guest snapshots may impose substantially different compatibility obligations.

Concept requirement: before adopting a mechanism, define who owns upstream security review and who owns recovery of retained state after runner, guest image, kernel or save-format changes. State the supported recovery lifetime and the outcome when a retained generation cannot use the current backend. Choose the persistence mechanism with that obligation visible; do not let importing a launcher implicitly choose the product’s saved-state policy.

Later proof: document the actual dependency closure, exercise retained generations across the supported upgrade combinations and verify rollback or explicit refusal. The inspected source supports useful mechanisms—quiescence checks, fenced identity changes and atomic local publication—but establishes no task-level cross-worker recovery guarantee (`SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/supervisor/src/service/execution.rs:90–143`; `SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/supervisor/src/execution_store.rs:92–117`).

These requirements preserve the stated journeys: HTTP-only review, local-tool review of exact revisions after subsequent pushes, queued follow-ups, conversation compaction, private coding sessions across leases, approval-led repair, overlapping incidents, independent monitoring fleets, bounded drafts and human-controlled merge and deployment (`concepts_brief.md:56–145`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:178–401`). They do not require completed implementation evidence before further concept refinement.

The concept is coherent enough for brainstorming. This lens found no Blocker in the proposed ownership boundary. The main unresolved risks concern session lifetime, approval authority and serial diagnosis capacity. Missing implementation and benchmarks are later proof needs, not defects in this concept review.

Dimension throughout: Contrarian / You Aren’t Gonna Need It (YAGNI) and Code Minimization. SPACE means Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution.

All project references below resolve under `/Users/kishore/Projects/agentsfleet-approved-fleet-chat`. SPACE references resolve under `/Users/kishore/Projects/oss/rs/SPACE`.

1. **Major — Session durability needs a bounded lifetime independent of fleet holds.**

   **Targets:** `concepts_brief.md:129–135`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:124–175`.

   The proposal correctly distinguishes task workspaces from compute, but retention duration, file coverage and capacity remain open. These choices determine whether “continue incident A after working on B” is a useful promise. Retaining unfinished sessions indefinitely creates an unbounded storage obligation; retaining only a fleet’s recent generations can evict an unrelated incident.

   **Supporting evidence:** Current `HoldKey` contains fleet, account workspace, limits and policy, with no task or incident identity (`rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/holds/mod.rs:36–49`). Reused holds skip checkout (`rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/lease_loop/workspace.rs:66–83`). Existing architecture describes a proposed retention policy of three snapshots per fleet (`docs/architecture/runner_execution.md:355`), which does not establish retention for several independent unfinished sessions.

   **Counterargument:** The evaluation already names this gap and requires separate attachment identity. That is appropriate concept work; durable recovery need not already exist.

   **Concept requirement:** Decide which entity owns retained generations and how unfinished, completed, expired and deleted sessions differ. Set numerical limits for retained bytes, session count, checkpoint frequency and promised retention. Decide what users experience when capacity is exhausted. Reuse fleet leases for worker ownership; the session record need not become another scheduler.

   **Later proof:** Preserve A’s local commits, index state and declared untracked files through A-to-B-to-A switching, hold expiry and worker replacement. Include storage exhaustion and deletion without silently evicting another unfinished task.

2. **Major — “Owner approval” lacks a precise existing principal.**

   **Targets:** `concepts_brief.md:88–100`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:279–293`.

   “Owner,” “permitted approver” and “fleet ownership” are not yet interchangeable concepts. Choosing a fleet creator, account owner or designated approver changes both the user journey and the amount of identity machinery required. Slack routing cannot make that choice.

   **Supporting evidence:** The fleet table records workspace and tenant ownership, without a per-fleet human owner field (`schema/1500_fleet_fleets.sql:11–32`). Existing roles describe account ownership and membership (`rustd/crates/afd_tenant/src/workspace/access.rs:15–32`). Members currently reach ordinary approvals (`docs/AUTH.md:300–315`). The inspected Slack path resolves team, subscribers and addressed fleet before admission; it does not establish the responding person’s account-owner role (`rustd/crates/afd_api_ingress/src/handler/mention/mod.rs:231–277`).

   **Counterargument:** The evaluation explicitly acknowledges missing identity checks. The objection is the unresolved meaning of approval authority, not an expectation that the checks already be implemented.

   **Concept requirement:** Name the existing principal or explicitly proposed delegation that may approve this handoff, and how a Slack user becomes verifiably associated with it. Keep this decision local to the proposed repair approval unless a broader permission change is explicitly intended. Do not introduce a new fleet ownership system merely because the prose says “owner.”

   **Reuse boundary and later proof:** Existing approval machinery supplies useful decision and admission vocabulary, but its current behavior is not a drop-in implementation. It updates the decision before a separate continuation path, and that continuation targets the original fleet (`rustd/crates/afd_approval/src/inbox/resolve/mod.rs:81–98,125–145,185–205`). The proposal instead finishes the responder and admits the repairer (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:329–331`). Later proof must cover interrupted approval-to-admission publication, simultaneous chat and Slack replies, changed authority and the wrong incident.

3. **Major — Durable admission does not establish useful monitoring latency.**

   **Targets:** `concepts_brief.md:108–117`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:305–351,369–378`.

   Keeping one active lease per fleet is consistent with current ownership. Its suitability for critical monitoring remains an unanswered product question. A durable accepted alert can still wait behind a long diagnosis. Adding several monitoring fleets helps only when responsibility and alert routing are defined; overlapping subscriptions can produce duplicate diagnoses.

   **Supporting evidence:** Selection takes each fleet’s oldest unsettled admission (`rustd/crates/afd_fleet/src/lease/sql/lease/select_ledger_candidates.sql:27–39`). The architecture explicitly provides no global waiting-time guarantee and allows 10,000 unsettled admissions per fleet (`docs/architecture/datastore_scaling.md:213–225`). The existing responder checks every fifteen minutes (`docs/architecture/scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md:34`).

   **Counterargument:** Serial diagnosis may be entirely sufficient for the intended workload. No evidence here establishes a need for more concurrent leases or another scheduler.

   **Concept requirement:** Obtain a numerical maximum for accepted critical-alert-to-diagnosis-start delay, separate from scheduled symptom-discovery delay. Bound diagnosis occupancy, evidence volume and acceptable repair backlog. Use those requirements to assess the existing serial model before changing concurrency. Leave cross-fleet incident ownership explicit when several monitors contribute evidence.

   **Later proof:** Inject another outage during a busy diagnosis and during an approval wait. Measure its start delay and confirm correct incident attribution. No such runtime measurement was performed for this review.

4. **Nit — Keep the native engine experiment independently useful from incident product expansion.**

   **Targets:** `concepts_brief.md:56–117,162–164`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:403–412`.

   The scope contains several independently valuable changes: conversation handoff, task-scoped files, revision-aware reviews, approval-led repair, incident grouping and a new guest engine. A native engine alone cannot establish the other outcomes. Making them one indivisible delivery would make both failures and benefits difficult to attribute.

   **Supporting evidence:** The current reviewer uses supervisor HTTP tools without a sandbox (`docs/architecture/scenarios/github-pr-reviewer.md:54–56`). The current repairer writes Git objects through HTTP without a checkout (`docs/architecture/scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md:48–56`). Existing execution boundaries already separate engine preparation from sandbox execution (`rustd/crates/afr_sandbox/src/engine/mod.rs:155–175`; `rustd/crates/afr_executor/src/api/mod.rs:246–263`). Trusted checkout currently requires a host-visible workspace (`rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/lease_loop/checkout.rs:33–55`).

   **Concept refinement:** Identify the first bounded mechanism and its independently observable benefit. Keep HTTP-only reviews and diagnosis, repeated revision checks, approval handoff, separate incidents and native tested repairs in the overall scope; avoid making all of them prerequisites for evaluating guest launch or file recovery. The owner’s chosen direction of local control does not require copying a larger upstream subsystem first.

   **Later proof:** Compare equivalent correctness and recovery behavior before comparing latency. The stated concurrency levels of 1, 10 and 100 are proposed workloads, not product budgets or observed capacity (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:454–456`).

5. **Nit — Two suggested SPACE reuse candidates already have local counterparts.**

   **Targets:** `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:422–439`.

   **Atomic publication:** Local report spooling already writes a temporary file, synchronizes it, publishes it and synchronizes the containing directory (`rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/report_spool/mod.rs:107–115`). SPACE’s execution store uses the same publication sequence (`SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/supervisor/src/execution_store.rs:92–117`). Its stored value is an execution identity in a host-local directory, not a durable repository checkpoint (`execution_store.rs:20–24,62–89`).

   **PostgreSQL classification:** Local billing already classifies lock and statement timeouts (`rustd/crates/afd_billing/src/error/mod.rs:157–175,196–200`). SPACE’s contention helper includes serialization and deadlock errors but deliberately treats query cancellation separately (`SPACE/crates/libs/postgres-contention/src/lib.rs:37–67`). These policies must not be substituted indiscriminately.

   **Reuse opportunity:** Prefer the existing local publication pattern where suitable, and adopt only the missing behavior. Require a concrete caller and retry policy before importing another error-classification abstraction. This supports the evaluation’s existing rejection of speculative storage-crate extraction (`docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:414`).

   **Later proof:** Upstream execution fencing and reconnect identity remain useful reference mechanisms, but copying their callers would bring additional runtime and transport dependencies. The supervisor manifest directly depends on upstream core, service and runtime crates (`SPACE/crates/libs/node/runtime/supervisor/Cargo.toml:32–35`). The complete launcher dependency closure remains **unverified**. Stable command identity and bounded result retention also require deliberate adaptation; upstream reconnect behavior is visible in `SPACE/crates/libs/data/plane/server/src/native/streams.rs:32–115`.

The strongest counterargument remains maintenance cost: local control transfers security fixes, dependency updates and operational failure handling to `agentsfleet`. The targets acknowledge that cost and correctly avoid claiming a measured winner (`concepts_brief.md:24–30`; `docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md:418–432,456`). No benchmark, build, test or service was run. No concept was marked finalized or ready for implementation.

# Native coding sandbox informed by SPACE

* **Author:** Aiwa, based on Kishore's inputs.
* **Date:** Oct 24, 2026
* **Status:** Working hypothesis for Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) brainstorming. Reviewers were started before the concept walkthrough and interrupted. No complete independent review is available.

## Overview

Build an `agentsfleet`-owned coding sandbox informed by SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution).
Study its approaches and adapt selected source where that improves our runner.
Keep performance tuning, behavior and future changes under our control.

The intended user can work on a repository through a fleet, follow its progress and continue after an interruption.
The owner's usual recovery expectation is conversation continuity, similar to continuing from compacted context.
Exact file recovery and running-process restoration still need explicit boundaries.

The [sandbox evaluation](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md) owns the technical evidence, reuse candidates and proposed coding walkthrough.
This brief records the working scope for review; no native backend or copied component is implemented by this brainstorm.

## Analysis

### The weakest assumption

Copying source gives us responsibility for performance; it does not prove that performance will improve.
Bringing in shared runtime dependencies can recreate the complexity of integrating a whole platform.
Every selection needs a bounded local role, failure proofs and measurements of the user's complete task.

The strongest counterargument is maintenance cost: an external service leaves more runtime maintenance upstream.
The owner prefers local control, so the proposal must account for security fixes, dependency updates and changes to copied code.
The [source-reuse criteria](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#selective-space-reuse) define what each candidate must explain before adoption.

### Ownership

Keep admission, current permissions and fleet scheduling with the existing daemon and trusted runner supervisor.
Fit the proposed guest engine behind the existing sandbox and executor boundaries.
Keep repository credentials outside untrusted code.

```text
User request and follow-ups
            |
Existing daemon and trusted runner supervisor
            |
      +-----+----------------------+
      |                            |
Conversation history        Repository preparation
and compaction                      |
      |                     Existing engine boundary
Authorized recovery                 |
      |                     Native coding sandbox
      +------ continue work -------+
```

The [existing ownership model](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#proposed-ownership) supplies the detailed boundaries.
A source copy must not introduce a second fleet scheduler or a competing owner of execution state.

### Coding session walkthrough

You bind a repository and ask a fleet to change its code.
For a run using local tools, the trusted supervisor prepares a private checkout and starts the proposed native guest engine.
The agent loop keeps conversation and model access outside the guest; commands and file edits run inside it.
An HTTP-only review can stay in the supervisor without starting a sandbox.

You see repository setup and command progress, then the resulting diff and actual test results.
Follow-up messages keep the existing queued ordering.
When context fills, shared compaction keeps the same task moving independently of the guest engine.

After worker loss, the proposed recovery path reloads authorized conversation state and checks the available repository and command outcomes before continuing.
Exact recovery of uncommitted files and running processes remains an open design question.
The [detailed coding walkthrough](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#walkthrough-to-build-and-test) owns the failure cases and required proof.

### Existing repository and incident journeys

The [existing reviewer scenario](docs/architecture/scenarios/github-pr-reviewer.md) and [production repair scenario](docs/architecture/scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md) already describe these product journeys.
The [repeat-review flow](docs/architecture/lease_flow.md#5-the-pr-is-fixed-and-pushed-again) covers a laptop push waking the same fleet again.
Use those pages as the foundation rather than inventing a separate workflow.

For a pull request, pin each review to its exact head and base commits, then recheck earlier findings against subsequent pushes.
Conversation history can retain the reasoning, while the checkout changes to the newly verified code revision.
Review posting remains blocked by current egress rules.

For an incident, distinguish the failed workflow commit, deployed revision and current `main` before choosing a patch base.
The proposed sandbox path reproduces and tests a bounded fix, then presents a draft pull request under the existing publication limits.
The current incident repairer writes through GitHub APIs without a checkout; a tested native sandbox patch path remains proposed.

The [revision walkthroughs](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#repository-revisions-across-events) own the preparation rules, gaps and failure proofs.
Incident linkage and post-deploy verification remain unimplemented as identified there.

### Approve a diagnosed repair from chat or Slack

The owner proposes showing the completed diagnosis and a repair proposal in fleet chat or a configured Slack thread.
Patch work waits for an authorized response that identifies that proposal.
In Slack, the person addresses the repair fleet and asks it to fix the diagnosed issue.

Chat approval and the Slack reply must resolve the same recorded action; retries or answers in both channels cannot create another repair run.
Approval starts a fresh run under current authority, after checking that the evidence and code still support the proposed plan.
The [approval walkthrough](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#owner-approval-in-chat-or-slack) owns the fields, authority boundaries and failure cases.

Existing Slack routing supports addressed repair requests, but does not alone prove the responder owns the fleet.
Owner identity checks and a proposal shared across both channels remain proposed implementation work.
Existing repository grants still bound every action, and merge and deployment remain separate decisions.

### Overlapping outages

Keep the monitoring responder and repairer fleets across outages, with a separate conversation, evidence and approval for each incident.
Repeated symptoms update the same incident when evidence supports that grouping; unrelated outages stay separate.
Provider logs remain outside the conversation, which keeps bounded evidence and references.

Waiting for an owner must release the responder so another outage can be diagnosed while the separate repairer works.
Preserve one active run per fleet: another approved repair queues unless separately configured repairer fleets supply concurrent capacity.
The [overlapping incident walkthrough](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#several-incidents-under-the-same-fleets) owns the proposed grouping, queue and recovery boundaries.

A single monitoring fleet also diagnoses outages one at a time; separate conversations do not add concurrent runs.
Several separately saved monitoring bots are separate fleets and can run concurrently when their respective triggers fire.
The [multi-bot walkthrough](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#several-monitoring-bots-and-their-triggers) distinguishes scheduled checks, routed alerts and duplicate diagnoses from overlapping subscriptions.

Existing admission accepts additional work while a fleet is busy, subject to backlog limits; the next diagnosis still waits for its turn.
Set the maximum acceptable diagnosis start delay for another critical outage before deciding whether serial fleet runs satisfy the monitoring goal.

### Conversation recovery and sandbox recovery

Compaction keeps useful context inside the model window while original history remains available.
Worker loss additionally requires checking which files and command outcomes actually survived.
A summary describing an edit cannot establish that its exact bytes remain available.

The [recovery hypothesis](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#conversation-recovery-working-hypothesis) gives conversation continuity priority while keeping those distinctions explicit.
Existing runtime checkpoints include a lease and branch identity; another worker needs an authorized recovery path.
An uncertain external action needs verification before any retry.

The proposed coding session keeps its own repository workspace across leases, including saved local commits and uncommitted work.
Ending a lease or waiting for approval may release compute, while a completed durable checkpoint retains the task's work.
The [session walkthrough](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#coding-sessions-and-worktrees-across-leases) owns attachment identity, save ordering, retention limits and the worker replacement proof.

Incident A and incident B need separate writable workspaces even when one fleet handles both in sequence.
Current temporary sandbox holds do not provide durable workspace recovery; this remains proposed integration work.
Save coverage, checkpoint frequency and retention duration still need explicit limits.

### Performance and concurrency

Measure the complete path from request through repository preparation, setup and the first useful command.
Measure save and recovery separately, with both unused and cached environments and concurrent requests for the same repository.
Compare candidates only after they meet the same isolation, authorization and recovery requirements.

The [measurement plan](docs/architecture/sandbox_evaluation.md#performance-and-failure-measurements) records the workloads and failure cases.
No local SPACE runtime benchmark establishes a performance winner.
The owner has not yet set numerical latency, resource or cost budgets.

## Goals vs. Non-Goals

* **In-Scope Goals:** A native sandbox design with selective source reuse, explicit ownership, tenant isolation, bounded execution, measured concurrency and conversation-led recovery.
* **In-Scope Goals:** Explain which SPACE mechanisms to copy, adapt or rebuild, including every dependency and the maintenance burden.
* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:** Operating SPACE as the product's sandbox service or broadly importing its lifecycle and control plane.
* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:** A second fleet scheduler, changed follow-up ordering, or a blanket promise that conversation context restores files and processes.
* **Out-of-Scope Non-Goals:** Changing the approved compaction-before-Billing delivery order or claiming the existing pull request is ready.

## Key Decisions & Staging for Next Steps

The owner wants SPACE's approaches and useful source adapted into a sandbox we maintain and can change.
Conversation continuity is the usual recovery priority.
Compaction remains application-owned and independent of the sandbox backend.
The proposed incident handoff waits for the owner's response to a diagnosis-linked repair proposal in chat or Slack.

Before implementation, settle the first reusable mechanism, supported host requirements, file recovery boundaries and measurable performance budgets.
Specify how recent conversation and tool outcomes become durable, and how replacement workers obtain current authority.
Record how upstream fixes reach each copied component.

Walk through this hypothesis with the owner and confirm readiness before launching independent Goldfish reviews.
Those reviews evaluate this concept; they do not reopen or replace the terminal implementation review recorded for pull request 784.
Retain reviewer findings and unresolved objections when refining the final brief.

# Coding sandbox evaluation

> Read this to evaluate SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) approaches and source for an `agentsfleet`-owned coding sandbox. The [working concept brief](../../concepts_brief.md) records the brainstorming scope. [Runner execution](runner_execution.md) owns implemented execution behavior; [conversation compaction](context_lifecycle.md) owns model context. Native sandbox changes and durable workspace recovery remain proposals.

## Recommendation and decision criteria

Build an `agentsfleet`-owned sandbox using selected SPACE approaches and source where they solve an observed problem.
The owner requires control over sandbox performance and future changes.
Finish shared compaction independently of sandbox implementation.

Use SPACE as a studied reference, with each code selection reviewed against our existing runner boundaries.
Keep its service as a comparison baseline; operating that service is outside the current direction.
No component has been selected for copying or implemented by this brainstorm.

Use isolation, recoverable work, authorization, end-to-end latency and operational ownership as the decision criteria. Isolation and authorization are pass/fail requirements. Compare performance only after each option satisfies the same recovery behavior. No local SPACE runtime benchmark has been run for this evaluation.

| Option | Benefit | Cost or gap | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Improve the existing engine | Uses the existing runner and directly addresses repeated context work and repository contention. | The implemented bubblewrap engine shares the host kernel; durable remote workspace recovery remains a target. | Baseline and preparation work. |
| Operate SPACE behind its HTTP API | Reuses its Firecracker lifecycle, storage and process transport. | Adds a platform to operate; requires authorization mapping, remote checkout and recovery integration. | Comparison baseline, outside the current direction. |
| Adapt selected SPACE approaches and source | Keeps sandbox behavior and performance under our control within the existing runner. | We own integration, updates and every dependency brought in with copied code. | Owner-selected design direction; evaluate components individually. |
| Copy its lifecycle/control plane broadly | Reuses more implementation at once. | Creates overlapping scheduling, tenancy and recovery ownership; effectively maintains a platform fork. | Outside the current direction. |

The current implementation and missing capabilities are recorded in [runner execution's Facts table](runner_execution.md#facts).
SPACE records desired state in PostgreSQL and reconciles workers directly or through Kubernetes; Kubernetes is optional.
Its service compatibility policy excludes Rust crate interfaces, so internal source reuse carries a separate maintenance burden.
See upstream [request flow](https://github.com/perplexityai/SPACE/blob/20d321385dac0855b39f86cd93c008ff5ec4ce3c/docs/architecture.md#request-and-execution-flow) and [versioning](https://github.com/perplexityai/SPACE/blob/20d321385dac0855b39f86cd93c008ff5ec4ce3c/docs/versioning.md).

## What the Claude session reference establishes

The owner supplied an inside-the-guest report from Oct 22–24, 2026. It is useful evidence about one environment. Keep its observations separate from proposed explanations.

| Evidence supplied | Supported reading | Still unproved by that observation |
|---|---|---|
| Hypervisor flag and a container detector reporting Docker | Virtualized execution and a detected container environment. | The hypervisor implementation, host placement and session-to-machine mapping. |
| Kernel build name includes `fc` | Firecracker is a plausible explanation. | A kernel build label does not identify the running virtual machine monitor. |
| New boot/kernel, same repository files | Files were preserved or reconstructed across that transition. | Disk reattachment versus snapshot restoration, synchronization or another mechanism. |
| Proxy variables and a certificate bundle | Applications are configured to use a proxy. | Enforcement against direct sockets, alternate protocols or modified environment variables. |
| Device size exceeds reported available space | Capacity accounting needs investigation. | The particular quota or storage layout. |
| A long-lived agent process and `--stdin` supervisor flag | A resident process and an input-related supervisor option. | Message framing, durable acknowledgement and interruption ordering. |

Anthropic's [cloud documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web#security-and-isolation) separately describes isolated session virtual machines and a Git proxy that keeps credentials outside the guest. Its [expiry guidance](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web#environment-expired) restores conversation history into fresh compute while background work may have stopped. Neither identifies its hypervisor or disk recovery implementation.

A container inside a microVM can make userland reproducible. It is an optional packaging choice for this proposal. A guest image with a restricted executor may satisfy that need without operating Docker inside every guest. Test whichever packaging we select against actual tools and privileges.

## Proposed ownership

```text
 User: repository + request + follow-ups
                    |
         agentsfleetd: admission and current authority
                    |
       trusted runner supervisor, outside tenant code
          |                         |
   shared context lifecycle    coding workspace preparation
          |                         |
   model calls and notes       Engine / Sandbox / Executor
          |                      /                 \
   guarded checkpoint       bubblewrap       native guest engine
   publication                                      |
                                          Firecracker guest
                                          tools + private files

   Git credentials remain in a trusted broker/proxy.
   A sandbox handle never grants fleet or repository authority.
```

Keep the fleet as the durable runtime. A workspace handle is an execution resource, not a second task scheduler. Preserve the existing one-active-lease rule. Independent coding tasks need independent writable checkouts; sharing an authorized read cache must not share mutable working trees.

The existing [engine interfaces](../../rustd/crates/afr_sandbox/src/engine/mod.rs) and [executor](../../rustd/crates/afr_executor/src/api/mod.rs) already separate execution effects. However, [checkout](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/lease_loop/checkout.rs) requires a host-visible workspace. A remote engine therefore needs a repository preparation path; implementing `Executor` alone is insufficient.

Use traits for effects with distinct implementations. Use generics for known adapters and trait objects where the backend is selected at runtime. Use `Fn` for a repeatable cancellation observation, `FnMut` for progress accumulation and `FnOnce` for consuming prepared publication. These choices express ownership; additional trait layers do not themselves improve concurrency.

## Walkthrough to build and test

Use a synthetic Git repository with a pinned base commit, a small build, an existing test and one requested behavior change. Keep real user repositories out of destructive recovery tests. Give each run its own namespace and retain only task-owned artifacts.

| Step | User action or injected event | Required observable result | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bind a repository and ask for the change. | Record the exact base commit and current repository permission; create one private writable checkout. | Repository hash, clean initial diff and denied foreign repository access. |
| 2 | Start work and perform setup. | Report progress for checkout, environment setup and the first useful command separately. | Stage timings and a command result; a live machine alone is insufficient. |
| 3 | Send a follow-up while a command is running. | Acknowledge the queued steer event; finish the current run before leasing that event. Show queued versus consumed status. | A controlled command barrier proves the follow-up does not start a second active lease and runs after the first. Mid-run steering is a separate proposed behavior. |
| 4 | Grow both setup and runtime context through repeated compaction. | Continue with the goal, latest instructions and complete tool groups; retain original source history. | Forced host tests plus the unchanged full continuity journey. Turn count alone does not prove a compaction occurred. |
| 5 | Edit tracked files, create an untracked file and leave a local commit unpushed. | Report which checkpoint durably protects each item and its recovery boundary. | Hashes, Git status and the committed workspace manifest; no assumption that Git commit captures all files. |
| 6 | Suspend, then replace the worker after a completed durable save. | Restore the declared files and base commit under a new current lease. Reject stale writers. Report processes as restored or stopped according to the chosen mechanism. | Restore on a different worker; compare hashes and reject an old lease's mutation. |
| 7 | Drop a command attachment after its side effect, then reconnect. | Reattach to the existing command or report uncertain outcome. Never automatically start the side effect again. | Append a unique marker once; interrupt transport after acknowledgement and count markers after reconnect. |
| 8 | Review the diff and run verification. | Show only this task's changes and actual test output. Recheck current permission before any authorized push. | Exact diff, test result and a separate permission-revocation test. |

Steps 5–7 describe required future workspace/backend behavior, not capabilities proved by the current compaction work. A supervisor restart additionally requires application conversation recovery; restoring a guest cannot restore an agent loop running outside it.

[Existing steer semantics](runner_fleet.md#steer-kill-pause) queue a human message for the next run. The supplied Claude reference observes consumption during the current agent task. Adopting a sandbox backend does not change that product behavior. Test the existing ordering first; changing it requires a decision about partial tool effects, ordering, interruption and model-request cancellation.

Keep these recovery units distinct:

| Recovery unit | Authority and purpose | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Conversation checkpoint | Application-owned summary and validated source coverage. | Existing runtime notes are lease/branch scoped. A replacement lease needs an explicitly authorized recovery path; an old checkpoint cannot grant access. |
| Workspace checkpoint | Proposed private file state, manifest, base commit and generation. | It protects only the last successfully published durable generation. A hard crash before that boundary can lose later writes. |
| Resident pause | Backend keeps stopped compute and local files. | It consumes resources and does not establish host-loss durability. |
| Machine snapshot | Backend saves memory, runtime state and disk according to its lifecycle. | It can contain stale credentials, sockets and ownership state; restore requires current authorization. |
| Git push or artifact export | Explicit publication outside the temporary execution environment. | A Git push excludes untracked files, dependencies and process state. |

SPACE explicitly distinguishes resident pause from persisted suspend and warns that acknowledged file writes may be lost before lifecycle persistence boundaries. Its semantics need to be reflected in our user-visible save status. See upstream [persistence](https://github.com/perplexityai/SPACE/blob/20d321385dac0855b39f86cd93c008ff5ec4ce3c/docs/architecture.md#lifecycle-and-persistence).

### Conversation recovery working hypothesis

The owner's working expectation is to recover the conversation and continue from its context, as during compaction.
Treat conversation continuity as the primary recovery requirement while the remaining boundaries are clarified.

Worker loss also requires checking the files available to the replacement runner.
A summary can describe a completed edit without retaining its exact bytes.
A command may have changed an external service even when its result never reached the conversation.

The recovery design must distinguish conversation progress, available file state and confirmed command outcomes.
For the proposed coding journey, retain saved uncommitted work and local commits across ordinary lease handoffs.
Conversation context alone cannot replace those bytes; exact save coverage, recovery frequency and retention duration still need a decision.
An uncertain external effect requires verification before any retry.

Current [runtime identity](../../rustd/crates/afr_agent/src/loop/context/mod.rs) binds notes to a lease and branch.
Cross-worker conversation recovery needs an authorized handoff and retained source history; compaction alone does not supply that path.

### Coding sessions and worktrees across leases

The proposed coding session owns a task's conversation and repository workspace across several leases.
A lease gives one runner temporary authority to work on that session; several model and tool turns can happen within one lease.
Renewing a lease or compacting context must preserve that session's working files.

Identify the session by its owning workspace, fleet, task or incident, and repository.
Resuming incident A selects A's saved workspace; diagnosing incident B selects a separate workspace when local code tools are required.
The session records work and recovery state, without assigning workers or replacing fleet scheduling.

```text
Incident A / coding session A / private Git workspace A
      lease 1 -> saved generation 1 -> owner approval wait
                                      |
      lease 2 <-----------------------+ restore or verified reattach
      lease 2 -> saved generation 2 -> tested patch

Incident B / coding session B / private Git workspace B
```

The current [workspace implementation](runner_execution.md#workspace-between-leases) keeps only a temporary fleet-scoped hold; durable save and restore are not built.
Its [hold key](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/holds/mod.rs) names the fleet, workspace, limits and policy, without incident identity.
The proposed session identity must participate in attachment checks so a same-fleet incident cannot inherit another incident's writable checkout.

At a planned handoff, stop workspace writers before recording a consistent file checkpoint.
Save the base commit, local commits, staged and unstaged edits, declared untracked files and the metadata needed to reconstruct the repository.
Upload complete checkpoint content before publishing its manifest and current generation under the live lease's authority.

Linked Git worktrees refer to administrative data outside their working directory, as the [Git worktree details](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree#_details) explain.
Copying that directory alone can leave broken references after a host change.
The save format must retain required Git objects and state, or reconstruct a private checkout with equivalent contents and index state.

Record which conversation progress and command outcomes correspond to the saved workspace generation.
A new lease checks current authority and resumes that recorded point; it cannot reuse expired credentials or another lease's write permission.
Use current lease fencing and workspace generation checks to refuse stale writes and checkpoint publication.

The runner may reuse compatible compute or release it after a confirmed durable save.
Ending a lease, serving incident B or waiting for approval must not delete the only recoverable copy of A's saved work.
Warm attachment is an optimization; recovery must also work after the old worker disappears.

SPACE's resident pause and durable suspend distinction is useful here; select its save, publication and cleanup mechanisms individually.
An adopted mechanism must satisfy our file recovery rules, regardless of whether it saves a filesystem or a complete guest snapshot.
Restoring files does not promise that background commands are still running.

If a planned save fails, mark the session as not durably saved and do not report a recoverable handoff.
Retain the working copy where possible; a hard crash can still lose changes newer than the last completed checkpoint.
Show the saved generation and any recovery loss instead of claiming the latest work survived.

An authorized deletion or a declared retention policy removes durable session data.
An idle compute timeout can release compute while retaining the session's saved work.
Retention duration, retained file coverage and checkpoint frequency remain open; an unfinished task must not silently become an expired cache entry.

Extend the [coding walkthrough](#walkthrough-to-build-and-test) with an A-to-B-to-A handoff after hold expiry and replacement of the worker.
Verify local commits, index state, file hashes and untracked files; inject a failed save and a stale lease attempting publication or deletion.
These are required acceptance proofs for the proposed integration, not capabilities already supplied by the current runner or compaction work.

## Repository revisions across events

These proposed sandbox journeys extend existing scenarios; their current behavior remains owned by those pages.
The [pull request reviewer](scenarios/github-pr-reviewer.md) and [production deployment repair](scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md) provide the starting points.
[Repeated review](lease_flow.md#5-the-pr-is-fixed-and-pushed-again) already describes a laptop push waking the same fleet through a new event.

Fleet identity, conversation continuity and repository revision have separate lifetimes.
A continuing conversation must identify the exact code revision it describes.
A cached sandbox cannot establish that its files match a new event.

### Review a pull request after another laptop push

```text
Branch A at commit 1 -> review commit 1 -> findings
           |
Author edits locally and pushes commit 2
           |
Signed synchronize event -> next fleet run -> review commit 2
```

Keep the existing same-fleet queue ordering; the next event waits for the running lease to finish.
Before review, resolve the currently open pull request and its authorized repository, base and exact head commit.
Record the event's advertised head separately from the commit actually selected for review.

For review requiring local tools, the trusted supervisor fetches and materializes that exact commit in a private checkout.
Verify the checked-out commit before any tool runs; never merge a remote branch into an older review workspace.
An HTTP-only review can read pinned code and diffs without starting a sandbox.

Treat previous findings as review history scoped to the repository and pull request, with the reviewed commit recorded.
Recheck each finding against the new code and inspect the complete current change.
An incremental comparison may help, but cannot substitute for a full review after rewritten history or a changed base.

Before posting a result, reread the current head and label which commit the findings cover.
A result for an older commit cannot approve a newer commit.
Read remote review state after an ambiguous post before repeating it.

**Current gaps:** [Review posting is refused](lease_flow.md#4-how-agent-bob-01-can-reply), and prior review continuity across events is not automatic.
The [ingress digest](../../rustd/crates/afd_api_ingress/src/handler/webhook/github/mod.rs) carries the head commit but omits the base commit.
The proposed revision selection and publication checks need implementation and narrowly scoped posting authority.

### Turn production evidence into a patch

```text
Scheduled Grafana scan or failed deployment workflow
           |
Diagnosis + verified environment and relevant commits
           |
Repair proposal in fleet chat or a configured Slack thread
           |
Owner approves that proposal
           |
Fresh authority/source checks -> repair run -> private repair checkout
           |
Reproduce -> bounded patch -> tests -> draft pull request
           |
Human merge -> existing deployment pipeline
```

The existing [incident scenario](scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md#1-start-one-incident) keeps the responder and repairer independent.
A diagnosis does not automatically wake the repairer; a failed workflow or human steer starts its run.
The owner proposes an explicit human handoff: show the completed diagnosis and repair proposal, then wait for approval before producing a patch.
For this proposed incident flow, a failed workflow supplies evidence and starts diagnosis; it does not approve patch generation.

The repairer rereads evidence and verifies the repository, environment, workflow and relevant commit before changing code.
A failed workflow commit may never have reached production.
The latest `main` commit may differ from both the failed build and the deployed revision.

Reproduce against the affected revision when evidence allows, then compare it with a freshly verified `main` revision.
If the issue remains, create a private repair branch from that recorded target revision and test the fix there.
Ambiguous deployment identity or a failure outside code ends diagnosis-only, following the existing scenario.

Keep the approved repository, target base and daemon-issued repair branch as publication boundaries.
Preserve the existing [remote reconciliation](scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md#3-diagnose-and-open-one-draft-pr) before retrying a branch or draft creation.
Existing repair publishes Git objects through bounded HTTP requests; publishing a locally tested sandbox patch still needs a trusted implementation.

If `main` advances during work, compare the patch against its new head before presenting it as applicable to current `main`.
Keep any validated patch and its original base available; do not silently overwrite local work.
A changed base requires renewed testing and current permission checks.

Human merge and the repository's deployment pipeline retain their existing roles.
[Incident linkage and post-deployment verification](scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md#4-keep-preview-evidence-without-calling-it-production) remain unimplemented.
A successful workflow alone cannot certify that the original production symptom is resolved.

### Owner approval in chat or Slack

Present the diagnosis, evidence references, affected environment, repository, target revision, intended fix and planned tests before asking to start patch work.
The proposal identifies the repair fleet and whether its scope includes opening a draft pull request.
Keep that proposal available after the diagnosis run ends; waiting for the owner must not keep a worker or guest occupied.

The owner can approve the proposal in fleet chat, or address the repair fleet in its configured Slack thread.
An illustrative Slack reply is `@agentsfleet repairer fix this`, with the actual bot and fleet names supplied by that workspace.
The [existing mention routing](scenarios/slack-incident-responder.md#4-routing-a-mention) already requires an addressed request for a write-bound fleet.

A diagnosis started from Slack uses its recorded reply thread.
A scheduled diagnosis needs a configured notification destination before its proposal can appear in Slack.
The [existing reply path](scenarios/slack-incident-responder.md#6-how-the-answer-comes-back) keeps that destination outside model control.

Both channels must resolve the same recorded proposal and admit at most one repair run for that approval.
Repeated clicks, retried Slack events and a second answer through the other channel must return the existing decision.
Record approval and repair admission together, so an acknowledgement cannot leave approved work without a queued run.

Resolve a typed approval or `fix this` against the exact proposal, fleet and conversation or Slack thread.
If several proposals could match, request the intended proposal instead of guessing.
Quoted thread content, a model summary or an unrelated mention cannot approve work.

Verify the responding person's authority before recording approval and recheck current repository grants before starting repair.
Existing [workspace roles](../AUTH.md#memberships-and-roles) permit ordinary approvals more broadly than the proposed owner-only handoff.
The [mention handler](../../rustd/crates/afd_api_ingress/src/handler/mention/mod.rs) resolves team, channel and fleet; that routing alone cannot establish fleet ownership.

Owner approval through Slack therefore needs a verified relationship between the Slack user and the permitted approver.
This authority check and the shared repair proposal record remain design work, rather than existing behavior.
Keep existing repository grants as the access ceiling; this proposed work approval cannot widen tools, repository reach or publication rights.

On approval, recheck the diagnosis and selected revision before preparing a fresh repair run under current authority.
If changed evidence or code invalidates the approved plan, refresh the proposal and request a new approval before patch work.
Denial, expiry, deletion or revoked authority must prevent a new repair admission.

The approved work is the stated patch, tests and any explicitly included draft pull request.
Merging and deployment retain their separate authorities.
The proposal is a work handoff and does not add a new scheduler or sandbox control plane.

### Several incidents under the same fleets

Keep the configured responder and repairer fleets across outages.
Each distinct outage gets a proposed incident record and its own conversation, evidence, repair proposal, approval and result.
Approval for one incident cannot start work for another.

One monitoring fleet handles diagnosis runs serially.
If diagnosis A occupies its active run, diagnosis B waits until that run finishes.
Separate incident conversations preserve context but do not add concurrent capacity to that fleet.

The fleet can receive more work while its diagnosis run is active.
Existing [admission](lease_flow.md#admission-commits-the-queue-row) records each accepted job before acknowledging it; pickup waits for the fleet's active slot.
The [backlog budgets](datastore_scaling.md#the-admissions-ledger-is-the-queue) bound acceptance, with a retryable refusal when capacity is exhausted.

```text
Diagnosis A running + alerts B and C arrive -> A keeps running; B and C queue
Diagnosis A finishes                       -> B can start; C stays queued
```

Queued work does not interrupt diagnosis A or create another active run for that fleet.
Durable arrival handling already exists; grouping those alerts into incidents and recovering each incident's conversation remain separate proposed capabilities.

Further evidence from the same ongoing outage updates that incident.
Use provider alert identity, service, environment and deployment evidence when deciding whether symptoms belong together; matching error text alone cannot merge incidents.
Keep uncertain cases separate, and link a recurrence after confirmed resolution to the earlier incident.

Logs continue growing in the observability provider.
Each bounded monitoring sweep reads scoped evidence windows and saves progress after recording the relevant evidence.
Keep evidence references and bounded excerpts in each incident conversation instead of appending the whole log stream.

After recording a diagnosis and proposal, finish the responder admission and release its lease.
Waiting for owner approval must not park the responder's queue head, which can [block later admissions](../../rustd/crates/afd_fleet/src/lease/sql/lease/select_ledger_candidates.sql).
The saved proposal waits independently; approval admits the configured repairer's work.

```text
Responder sweep -> incident A -> proposal A -> owner approves -> repairer run A
Responder sweep -> incident B -> proposal B -> owner approves -> repairer queue B
More A evidence -> incident A
```

The responder can handle another outage while the separate repairer works on the first.
The [one active lease per fleet](data_flow.md#one-active-lease-per-fleet--the-ownership-model) rule still bounds each fleet.
A busy responder delays its next sweep; scheduled monitoring does not promise continuous log tailing.

For this proposal, another approved repair queues while the same repairer is busy.
Separate, explicitly configured repairer fleets can work concurrently; an outage does not create a fleet by itself.
Every repair needs its own checked source revision and private writable workspace.

Evidence grouping is separate from repeated webhook delivery detection and does not replace existing admission ordering.
Incident records, grouping rules and incident-scoped recovery remain proposed work, alongside the shared owner approval record.
Monitoring delay, evidence limits and repair queue capacity still need explicit budgets before implementation.
First set the maximum acceptable delay from an accepted critical alert to the start of its diagnosis.
If serial diagnosis cannot meet that bound, revisit fleet concurrency explicitly before choosing a sandbox mechanism.

### Several monitoring bots and their triggers

Several monitoring fleets are a supported arrangement; one global monitoring fleet is not required.
Each separately saved monitoring bot is a fleet with its own setup, triggers, permissions, budget and queue.
The [existing two-fleet scenario](scenarios/two-fleets-github-slack.md#6-pickup-two-runners-two-leases) shows independent fleets running concurrently when worker capacity and permission checks allow.

| Monitoring arrangement | Work admitted and run |
|---|---|
| Several alerts target one fleet | Separate accepted jobs enter that fleet's queue; diagnosis runs happen one at a time. |
| Different alerts target different fleets | Each fleet receives its own jobs and can run concurrently with the others. |
| The same alert targets several fleets | Each targeted fleet can receive a job; several diagnoses may describe the same outage. |

For example, a payments monitor and a database monitor can diagnose their respective outages at the same time.
If both subscribe to the same broad alert feed, both can wake for one outage.
Another outage does not create another fleet or notify every existing fleet by itself.

The [existing incident scenario](scenarios/production-deploy-repair.md#1-start-one-incident) describes scheduled Grafana reads.
Each due schedule wakes its own fleet, even when another monitoring fleet is already running.
Reading Grafana with a credential does not itself create an incoming alert subscription.

For an alert-driven setup, define which approved alert route targets which monitoring fleet before promising selective wakeups.
The [generic webhook route](../../rustd/crates/afd_api_ingress/src/handler/webhook/source_route.rs) names one fleet and source; it does not infer alert kinds from arbitrary payloads.
Grafana alert validation, routing and incident grouping need their own design and delivery proof.

The proposed default is to assign a responsible monitor for each service and environment.
Additional monitors can contribute evidence, but cross-fleet incident ownership must be explicit before their diagnoses can share one repair proposal.
Existing delivery retry detection does not establish shared incident identity across fleets.

### Checkout freshness and proof

Current [held sandbox reuse](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/lease_loop/workspace.rs) skips checkout and retains the previous files.
Fresh [materialization](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/workspace_clone/checkout.rs) selects a branch tip rather than an event-pinned commit.
The [sandbox Git tool](../../rustd/crates/afr_tools/src/sandbox/git/mod.rs) refuses remote operations, so trusted preparation must own refresh.

The proposed preparation path must verify the selected commit even when compute is reused.
Use a fresh private checkout or a verified reusable view; preserve or refuse an incompatible dirty workspace.
Reuse an authorized immutable source cache while keeping writable files private to the run.

Required proofs include a push during review, rewritten branch history, a changed base and a dirty held workspace.
Also inject duplicate deliveries, lost post acknowledgements, revoked repository access and a fork outside approved reach.
For repair, test a failed build that never deployed, `main` advancing, ambiguous evidence and an already-created remote draft.
Record the reviewed, affected, patch-base and published commits independently in every result.
For proposal approval, test simultaneous chat and Slack replies, unauthorized responders, ambiguous threads, expired proposals and a changed diagnosis.
Restart after approval but before pickup and verify that the same repair admission remains available without creating another patch run.

For overlapping incidents, prove another outage remains discoverable while the first waits for approval or occupies the repairer.
Send several alerts while diagnosis A is active; verify accepted jobs remain queued and run within the chosen start-delay budget.
Inject repeated alerts, late evidence, an approval naming the wrong incident and worker loss between evidence recording and progress updates.
Verify bounded conversation input, separate incident recovery and progress through the repair queue.

## Refactor order and files

| Slice | Files or existing area | Change and proof |
|---|---|---|
| Shared preparation | `rustd/crates/afd_context/src/{plan,ports}.rs`, [preparation work tests](../../rustd/crates/afd_context/tests/work.rs) and existing planner tests | Reduce cumulative estimates, retain a final complete provider estimate and exact output safety, and reject stale source. A blocked summary must not block another conversation. |
| Runtime history | `rustd/crates/afr_agent/src/loop/{mod,conversation}.rs`, `loop/context/{mod,source,estimate}.rs`; proposed history-index module | One owned encoded-history index and borrowed views; invalidate the affected tail when pending input changes. Preserve complete tool groups and native continuation rules. |
| Authoring preparation | `rustd/crates/afd_authoring/src/model/context/`, `model/dispatch/{mod,funding}.rs`, existing funding/source-change integration tests | Reuse prepared input only with an exact source/authority witness after funding. Funding and model access stay outside datastore locks. |
| Repository preparation proposal | `rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/{lease_loop/checkout.rs,workspace_clone/}`, related checkout and concurrency tests | Separate trusted repository acquisition from local or remote materialization. Preserve credential isolation; publish an immutable source before shortening mirror lock duration. |
| Native backend experiment | Existing `afr_sandbox` engine/boot and `afr_executor` boundaries; proposed guest engine informed by SPACE | Map readiness, process identity, bounded streams, cancellation, network policy, quota and cleanup. Unsupported semantics must refuse explicitly. |

## Performance and failure measurements

The fitting-history work test counts groups passed to estimators, not tokens, physical requests or actual elapsed time. For 40 pages of 64 groups, repeated cumulative estimates visit `64 × (1 + 2 + ... + 40) = 52,480` groups for 2,560 source groups. It exposes repeated work. It does not quantify a throughput gain or a provider bill.

Target bounded estimator visits in that fixture, then measure elapsed preparation time and allocations separately. Geometrically spaced probes must never send unchecked input; a complete provider estimate still precedes dispatch. An owned immutable prefix may reuse verified history evidence; an arbitrary stored watermark is insufficient.

Repository performance needs its own comparison. The [mirror lock](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/workspace_clone/mod.rs) currently covers fetch and checkout; [materialization](../../rustd/crates/afr_supervisor/src/workspace_clone/checkout.rs) copies the mirror's objects. Benchmark many checkouts of one repository separately from independent repositories. Moving the lock without making the source immutable can introduce inconsistent checkouts.

Measure request-to-checkout-ready, first useful command, verified diff, durable save and cross-worker resume. Report model wait separately from local preparation, queueing, Git transfer, dependency installation and snapshot transfer. Compare cold and warm environments at concurrency 1, 10 and 100, with equal repository state, hardware, limits and cache policy.

Report median, 95th and 99th percentiles, failure counts, memory, processor time, disk bytes, storage transfer and bystander latency. Include failures in latency reporting rather than dropping them. Adopt a candidate only after the same correctness workload passes and its measured latency/cost fits the product budget; there is no measured adoption winner yet.

Inject cancellation, slow consumers, dropped acknowledgements, duplicate starts, worker death before and after save, revoked repository access, stale lease writes, full byte/inode quotas and cache poisoning. Reserve capacity for cleanup and control records, then verify actual recovery at capacity. Cache identities must include the appropriate tenant scope and build inputs; untrusted setup must not publish trusted shared cache state.

## Evidence and execution boundary

Run repository claims through existing Make targets: `make lint-all`, `make test-unit-all`, `make test-integration-rustd`, `make check-version`, and the unchanged `make acceptance-local`. Use `make test-runner-kernel` for the implemented Linux sandbox; it does not prove Firecracker or SPACE behavior. A selected remote backend needs a distinct real-backend workload wired into the appropriate Make lane before support is claimed.

Keep failure injection deterministic with barriers, controlled transport loss and synthetic repository contents. Preserve source hashes, process markers and sanitized stage timings. Clean up only the run's own resources. A browser mock, scripted provider or successful service creation cannot substitute for a real cross-worker recovery proof.

The compaction work regression currently fails before optimization; the independent blocked-summary proof passes. Their measured output is recorded in the active spec. Full acceptance remains incomplete, so this evaluation makes no readiness or concurrent-throughput claim.
